Developing with AI agents

Source: vignettes/articles/ai-agents.Rmd
ai-agents.Rmd

In Japanese

This article is for a contributor who works with an agent: a tool that edits files and runs commands in the repository. Two such tools are covered: the Claude desktop app (its Code tab) and VS Code with GitHub Copilot’s agent. This page gives what is the same for both. The steps for each tool are on its own page:

  • Set-up in the Claude desktop app
  • Set-up in VS Code with GitHub Copilot

Advice that is the article’s own, and not from a tool’s documentation, is said to be so.

1. What this article is for

Some pages already cover nearby ground. This one does not repeat them.

  • CONTRIBUTING.md and the architecture article give the rules: branches, labels, review, versioning.
  • Developing with an AI assistant is for a chat assistant that you give the AI developer manual.
  • This article is about the set-up of an agent, how to work with it, and how to check what it made.

One set-up serves the three packages, rtfreporter, tflspec and tflplanner, because one change often crosses them. Where a package differs, the text says so.

Two things are outside this article: writing analysis code for a study (see Asking an AI chat for a table’s plan code), and the AI kits that the packages ship for their users.

2. The environment

An agent installs branch builds and runs tests. If your own R library is on the path, a test can pass only because of a package that you happen to have installed. An install can also overwrite a package that you use for other work. So give the agent a separate work library and a separate work home.

  • R version. DESCRIPTION (Depends:) holds the minimum, not the version to use. The versions that are tested are in Development setup in CONTRIBUTING.md and in the CI matrix in .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml. Do not copy a version from this page.
  • Folders. Before the first R call, set R_LIBS_USER, HOME and the R_USER_* folders (R_USER_CACHE_DIR, R_USER_DATA_DIR, R_USER_CONFIG_DIR) to folders of the work area. This holds for a one-line Rscript -e call too. Set TMP, TEMP and TMPDIR as well, so that no file lands in the system temporary folder.
  • Windows. Setting HOME alone is not enough: R still finds the user library. Set R_LIBS_USER too.
  • Which R. Call the R that the project names, by its full path. Do not use whichever Rscript comes first on the path.

An example, with a fictional work folder C:/work/tfl. Make the folders first.

WORK_ROOT=C:/work/tfl
R_LIBS_USER=C:/work/tfl/lib
HOME=C:/work/tfl/home
R_USER_CACHE_DIR=C:/work/tfl/home/cache
R_USER_DATA_DIR=C:/work/tfl/home/data
R_USER_CONFIG_DIR=C:/work/tfl/home/config
TMP=C:/work/tfl/tmp
TEMP=C:/work/tfl/tmp
TMPDIR=C:/work/tfl/tmp

The work library starts empty. Fill it with the project’s R and these variables: install.packages() for the packages in Development setup in CONTRIBUTING.md, or devtools::install_dev_deps() in the clone (install devtools first).

Run the script below first in every session. It prints the facts that matter and stops if a library or folder outside the work area is in use. Set WORK_ROOT to the work folder before you run it. The page shows the script and does not run it.

Show code 
# check-env.R -- run first: Rscript check-env.R
# WORK_ROOT is the folder that holds the work library and the work home.
win <- .Platform$OS.type == "windows"
norm <- function(path) {
  p <- sub("/+$", "", normalizePath(path, winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE))
  if (win) tolower(p) else p   # drive and folder case do not matter on Windows
}
root <- Sys.getenv("WORK_ROOT")
if (!nzchar(root) || !dir.exists(root)) {
  stop("Set WORK_ROOT to an existing work folder first.", call. = FALSE)
}
root <- norm(root)
# TRUE for the root itself and for a path below it; "C:/work-old" is not.
under_root <- function(path) {
  p <- norm(path)
  nzchar(path) && (p == root || startsWith(p, paste0(root, "/")))
}

cat("R:", R.version.string, "\n")
cat("R home:", R.home(), "\n")
cat("Library paths:\n")
print(.libPaths())

for (pkg in c("rtfreporter", "tflspec", "tflplanner")) {
  loc <- system.file(package = pkg)
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", pkg, if (nzchar(loc)) loc else "(not installed)"))
}
for (pkg in c("testthat", "lintr", "roxygen2", "covr")) {
  ver <- tryCatch(as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)),
                  error = function(e) "(not installed)")
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", pkg, ver))
}

# The base library and the site library of this R are allowed and listed;
# every other library must be in WORK_ROOT.
allowed <- unique(c(.Library, .Library.site))
cat("Allowed (base and site):\n", paste0("  ", allowed, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
libs <- .libPaths()
libs <- libs[!norm(libs) %in% norm(allowed)]
outside <- libs[!vapply(libs, under_root, logical(1))]

# R_LIBS_USER must be set, and each folder in it must exist and be in WORK_ROOT.
# (.libPaths() leaves out a folder that does not exist.)
user_libs <- strsplit(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), .Platform$path.sep)[[1]]
bad_user <- length(user_libs) == 0L ||
  !all(vapply(user_libs, function(p) under_root(p) && dir.exists(p), logical(1)))

dirs <- Sys.getenv(c("HOME", "R_USER_CACHE_DIR", "R_USER_DATA_DIR",
                     "R_USER_CONFIG_DIR", "TMP", "TEMP", "TMPDIR"))
bad_dirs <- names(dirs)[!vapply(dirs, under_root, logical(1))]

if (length(outside) > 0L || bad_user || length(bad_dirs) > 0L) {
  if (length(outside) > 0L) {
    cat("Libraries outside WORK_ROOT:\n", paste0("  ", outside, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
  }
  if (bad_user) {
    cat("R_LIBS_USER is unset, missing, or outside WORK_ROOT.\n")
  }
  if (length(bad_dirs) > 0L) {
    cat("Folders outside WORK_ROOT (or unset):", paste(bad_dirs, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  }
  stop("A library or folder outside the work area is in use. Fix the environment first.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
cat("Environment OK.\n")

Data. Use fictional data only (Example Pharma) and the sample studies that the packages ship. Never put company, study or patient data in code, tests, issues, pull requests or an agent’s session.

3. What the harness holds

The harness is everything around the agent: its instructions, its reusable tasks, its permissions and the checks that decide.

Instruction files

Keep one source and short pointers to it, not three copies. The files are:

  • AGENTS.md: the shared orientation. This repository has one.
  • CLAUDE.md: read by Claude Code. This repository has one. It imports @AGENTS.md and adds the notes for Claude Code. Keep it that way.
  • .github/copilot-instructions.md: read by Copilot. This repository has one.

What they say should be short:

  • where the authoritative documents are (CONTRIBUTING.md, the architecture article, the AI developer manual);
  • which branch to work from;
  • what an agent must not touch: Version: in DESCRIPTION, NEWS.md and CHANGELOG.md;
  • the test and lint commands;
  • when to stop and ask.

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md at the start of each session. It reads AGENTS.md only when there is no CLAUDE.md, so a CLAUDE.md that wants the shared text imports it, as this repository’s does. Copilot in VS Code reads .github/copilot-instructions.md or AGENTS.md. Each set-up page shows how to confirm that the file was read. An instruction file is a request, not a lock: Claude Code’s documentation says so, and says that a hook is what blocks an action.

The pre-PR check as a reusable task

Both tools can keep a task that you start by name. The list is the same, so either tool makes the same check. It is a faster subset, to run on each change:

  1. Run the tests of the changed area.
  2. Run lintr::lint_package(). The result must be 0 lints.
  3. Check that every new pkg:: use or requireNamespace() call is declared in DESCRIPTION.
  4. When a change in tflspec can break tflplanner, run tflplanner’s tests too.
  5. Report each result in the pull request description, in the form the pull request template asks for.

This task is not the four pre-push checks of CONTRIBUTING.md: R CMD check --as-cran, devtools::test(), pkgdown::check_pkgdown() and lintr. CI runs the full set, and so does a maintainer before a release.

The Claude desktop app holds the task as a skill, and VS Code as a prompt file. The set-up pages show both. The repository ships the skill, as .claude/skills/pre-pr/SKILL.md; it has no prompt file.

Checks that decide

An agent’s judgment is not a check. These are:

  • testthat, run as in CONTRIBUTING.md;
  • lintr, with the repository’s .lintr;
  • R CMD check;
  • cran-readiness, which is run by hand before a CRAN submission (R CMD check --as-cran with the manual, URLs, spelling);
  • version-guard, a CI check that refuses a change of the version to a release position unless the pull request has the release label;
  • the lint workflow, which runs lintr in CI;
  • coverage, in test-coverage.yaml;
  • undeclared dependencies: search the diff for pkg:: and requireNamespace() and compare the names with DESCRIPTION.
  • a scan of the dependencies for known vulnerabilities. GitHub’s list of ecosystems that Dependabot supports has GitHub Actions, and no R row was found. This repository has no .github/dependabot.yml file today, and its security settings (read 2026-11-08) show Dependabot security updates and secret scanning as disabled. No scanner is set up for the R dependencies.

Checks on each edit

Some rules are better enforced at each edit than at the end: lint a changed R file, or refuse an edit to Version: in DESCRIPTION, to NEWS.md or to CHANGELOG.md. Claude Code does this with hooks. VS Code has hooks too, in Preview. The Claude page shows an example set, which is in .claude/ in the repository (in next now, and in main with the next merge). The VS Code page shows the format of a hook. Where a tool cannot do it, the pre-PR check and CI cover the same ground.

4. The workflow

The loop

Issue, branch, small pull request, CI, review, merge.

  • One change per pull request, with Closes #n in its description.
  • A contributor opens the pull request against main. A maintainer (a Collaborator, with write access) works on a topic branch that goes to next, which is merged to main about once a week (Branching & collaboration in CONTRIBUTING.md). AGENTS.md, which Copilot’s instructions point to, names main only, so a maintainer who uses Copilot follows CONTRIBUTING.md.
  • The description holds the User-visible change (for NEWS) text. The agent does not edit NEWS.md or the version.
  • The agent opens the pull request. It does not merge it. The pause for review is the point.

Test first

Ask the agent to write the test that fails before the fix, and to show it failing. Then it fixes the code. For a bug report, the reproduction comes first and goes into the issue or the pull request.

What an agent does well

  • Reproducing a problem and narrowing down its cause.
  • A mechanical edit across many files.
  • Writing tests.
  • Translating text under a rule that you state.
  • Bringing a branch up to date with its base (main, or next for a maintainer).

What a person must check

Whatever the agent reports:

  • The numbers in an output. Compare them with a count made another way (section 5).
  • Screens. Look at them in a real browser.
  • Design decisions, API names, and anything users see.
  • The next package. A change in one package must not break the one after it (rtfreporter, tflspec, tflplanner).
  • That “done” matches the commit. Read the diff, not the summary.

5. Checking the finished material

A table that looks right can still be wrong. The check is a comparison with numbers that you worked out without the package.

Hand-worked expected tables

Make a small fictional dataset (Example Pharma). Work out every count, percent and N by hand, once, and keep the result next to the test. The test compares the generated table with that result, cell by cell. It does not compare it with the code’s own earlier output.

An example: blank values

Data read from a .xpt file gives a missing character value as "", not NA. A table that counts causes then treats "" as a category. It prints an extra blank row, and its percents look right.

A test on in-memory data with NA passes and hides this. The hand-worked table, made from data that was written and read back as the study stores it, catches it.

The order

  1. Take the data as the study stores it (write it to .xpt and read it back).
  2. Make the expected table by hand.
  3. Run the package.
  4. Compare the two, cell by cell.
  5. Then a person looks at the page.

When a check has found a problem once, keep it as a regression test.

6. The two tools, feature by feature

Job Claude desktop app (Code tab) VS Code with Copilot
Standing instructions for the repository CLAUDE.md. AGENTS.md is read only when there is no CLAUDE.md, unless CLAUDE.md imports it. .github/copilot-instructions.md, or AGENTS.md.
A reusable task (the pre-PR check) A skill: .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, started with /name. A prompt file: .github/prompts/<name>.prompt.md, started with /name. It runs only in the Local harness, which is deprecated.
Running tests and lint Runs commands with its Bash tool. Runs commands in the integrated terminal (Local sessions).
What it may run without asking Permission rules and permission modes. Terminal auto-approve rules (chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove).
Checks on each edit Hooks in .claude/settings.json. Hooks (Preview) in .github/hooks/*.json.
Handing a piece of work to a helper Separate sessions run in parallel; with Worktree on, each has its own worktree. Subagents, which work in their own context.
Reading an Issue or a pull request gh in the terminal. The app shows a pull request’s CI status after you open it. gh in the terminal. The VS Code pages read for this set-up do not say how Copilot reads an Issue or a pull request.

The facts in this table come from the tools’ own documentation, read on 2026-11-08; the set-up pages link the pages. Two facts about the Claude app were seen in a test in the app, and the Claude page says which. Tools change fast, so check the tool’s documentation when a step does not work as written.
